procedural_history.originating_court: The case originated as Writ Petitions (Nos. 289 to 295 of 1971) directly in the Supreme Court of India under Article 32 of the Constitution of India.
procedural_history.impugned_order: The petitioners challenged the validity of detention orders.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: There were no High Court proceedings mentioned in the text.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court held that the detention of the petitioners was illegal, made the rule issued in all the writ petitions absolute, and directed the release of the petitioners.

directions: Directs the release of the petitioners forthwith, unless they are required in connection with any other case.

issue.issue_text: Whether there was an unexplained delay by the State in disposing of the representation made by the petitioners, and if so, whether this delay violated their constitutional right under Article 22(5).

facts: The petitioners, who were detained, made a representation against their detention on March 1, 1971.
The State government received the representation on March 3, 1971, and rejected it on March 20, 1971.
This resulted in a delay of 17 days between the receipt and disposal of the representation.
The State argued that the delay was necessary to collect information from other officials and was therefore justified.
The petitioners contended that this delay was unexplained and violated their constitutional rights.
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution guarantees a detenu the right to be afforded the earliest opportunity of making a representation against a detention order.
Previous Supreme Court decisions established that it is implicit in Article 22(5) that the State must consider and dispose of such representations as expeditiously as possible.
An unexplained delay in disposing of a detenu's representation renders the detention illegal, as it violates the constitutional right guaranteed under Article 22(5).
application: The Court first established that there was, in fact, a 17-day delay by the State in handling the representation.
It then evaluated the State's justification for the delay—the need to gather information.

The Court rejected this explanation as unsatisfactory, noting that the required information could have been obtained very quickly (within minutes) as the jail was located a short distance from the Secretariat.
Therefore, the Court found that the 17-day period was not necessary and the delay was unexplained.
Applying the established legal principle from its prior rulings, the Court determined that this unexplained delay constituted a failure by the State to dispose of the representation expeditiously.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the unexplained delay of 17 days in disposing of the petitioners' representation violated their constitutional right under Article 22(5). Consequently, the Court accepted the petitioners' argument and struck down the detention orders as illegal on this ground alone.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention were vague or devoid of particulars.

facts: The petitioners argued that the grounds for their detention were vague, which made it impossible for them to make an effective representation against the detention order.
application: The Supreme Court first noted that it was striking down the detention orders on a different, primary ground: an inordinate and unexplained delay by the government in considering the petitioners' representation.
Despite this, the Court briefly addressed the petitioners' argument regarding the vagueness of the detention grounds.
The Court stated that it was "prima facie satisfied that the grounds are neither vague nor devoid of particulars."
It also found that there were materials on which the detaining authority could have based the detention orders.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the argument that the grounds of detention were vague. Although the Court did not find it necessary to analyze this issue in detail because it had already decided to quash the detention on other grounds, it explicitly stated its prima facie view that the grounds were not vague or lacking in particulars.

arguments.issue_text: Whether there was an unexplained delay by the State in disposing of the representation made by the petitioners, and if so, whether this delay violated their constitutional right under Article 22(5).
appellant_arguments: There was a delay by the State in passing orders on the representation made by the petitioners.
The delay has not been properly explained by the State.
The State only made a bald statement about making inquiries but did not disclose details or correspondence.
Any delay in considering a representation is unconstitutional as it violates the fundamental right of a detenu under Article 22(5), which requires immediate action when personal liberty is at stake.
respondent_arguments: There has been no delay on the part of the Government in considering the representation and no violation of Article 22(5).
To properly dispose of the representation, certain information had to be collected from other officials.
Even if there was any delay, it has been properly explained in the counter-affidavit.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention were vague or devoid of particulars.
appellant_arguments: The grounds of detention were vague, devoid of particulars, and the matters mentioned in them were absolutely false.
respondent_arguments: The contention that the grounds were vague is absolutely unjustified.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: An unexplained delay by the appropriate authority in considering a detenu's representation is a violation of the constitutional right guaranteed under Article 22(5), and this circumstance by itself is a sufficient ground for holding the order of detention illegal.
obiter: Prima facie, the grounds for detention were neither vague nor devoid of particulars, and there were materials on which the detaining authority could have passed the detention orders.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: We are of the opinion that the contention of Mr. Manchanda that there has been a delay in the State in passing orders on the representation made by the petitioners and that the said de ay has not been properly explained by the State, has, in the circumstances of this case, to be accepted. In consequence, it fo!'.ows that there has been a violation of the constitutional right guaranteed under Art. 22 ( 5) to the petitioners. We are further of the view that the detention orders will have to be struck down on this short gr.ound.
legal_tests_applied: The appropriate authority is bound to consider the representation of the detenu as early as possible.
The appropriate Government itself is bound to consider the representation as expeditiously as possible.
There should not be any delay in the matter of consideration, and any delay must be properly explained.
The consideration of the representation by the appropriate authority is entirely independent of any action by the Advisory Board.
why_appellant_lost: The court was prima facie satisfied that the grounds of detention were neither vague nor devoid of particulars.
The petitioners' own representation dealt with every one of the matters mentioned in the grounds, indicating they understood them.
If there was any vagueness in the grounds, it was open to the petitioners to have asked for further particulars, which they did not do.
why_respondent_won: The court was prima facie satisfied that the grounds of detention were neither vague nor devoid of particulars.
The petitioners' own representation demonstrated that they understood the grounds of detention, as they addressed every matter mentioned.
The petitioners failed to exercise their option to ask for further particulars if they found the grounds to be vague.
policy_considerations: The personal liberty of a person is at stake. Any delay would not only be an irresponsible act on the part of the appropriate authority but also unconstitutional because the Constitution enshrines the fundamental right of a detenu to have his representation considered and it is imperative that when the liberty of a person is in peril immediate action should be taken by the relevant authorities.
